question:
The EMPLOYEES table has a column COMMISSION_PCT that is NULL for employees who do not earn commission.
Which function call correctly returns 0 for employees whose COMMISSION_PCT is NULL, and returns COMMISSION_PCT unchanged otherwise?

options.text: NVL2(commission_pct, 0, commission_pct)
NVL(commission_pct, 0)
NULLIF(commission_pct, 0)
COALESCE(0, commission_pct)

solution: B - NVL(commission_pct, 0)

question: Which two statements are true about the COALESCE function in Oracle SQL? (Choose TWO)

options.text: It returns the first non-NULL expression from its argument list.
It can accept only exactly two arguments, like NVL.
COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 5) returns 5.
It evaluates every argument in the list before returning a result, even after finding a non-NULL value.
COALESCE always requires at least three arguments, unlike NVL which requires exactly two.

solution: A - It returns the first non-NULL expression from its argument list. C - COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 5) returns 5.

options.text: DATA
ABAS
TABA
An error, because the start position cannot be negative.

solution: A - DATA

options.text: It returns the position of the third occurrence of the letter 'A' in the string.
It returns the number of times the letter 'A' appears in the string.
It returns the position of the first occurrence of 'A' starting the search from position 3.
It raises an error, because INSTR only accepts two arguments.

solution: A - It returns the position of the third occurrence of the letter 'A' in the string.

question: Which statement correctly pads the EMPLOYEE_ID column on the left with zeros so the result is always 6 characters wide?

options.text: SELECT LPAD(employee_id, 6, '0') FROM employees;
SELECT RPAD(employee_id, 6, '0') FROM employees;
SELECT LPAD(6, employee_id, '0') FROM employees;
SELECT PAD(employee_id, 6, '0') FROM employees;

solution: A - SELECT LPAD(employee_id, 6, '0') FROM employees;

options.text: An error, because TRIM cannot remove multiple characters at once.

question: Which two statements are true about the ROUND and TRUNC functions when applied to the number 125.783? (Choose TWO)

options.text: ROUND(125.783, 1) returns 125.8.
TRUNC(125.783, 1) returns 125.8.
TRUNC(125.783, 1) returns 125.7.
ROUND(125.783, -2) returns 200.
TRUNC(125.783) returns 126.

solution: A - ROUND(125.783, 1) returns 125.8. C - TRUNC(125.783, 1) returns 125.7.

options.text: 2 and 17
2 and 0
3 and 17
An error, because MOD cannot be used with a divisor of 0.

solution: A - 2 and 17

question: Which statement is true about the CEIL and FLOOR functions in Oracle SQL?

options.text: CEIL(-10.5) returns -10, and FLOOR(-10.5) returns -11.
CEIL(-10.5) returns -11, and FLOOR(-10.5) returns -10.
CEIL and FLOOR both round to the nearest integer, choosing whichever is closer.
CEIL can only be used with positive numbers.

solution: A - CEIL(-10.5) returns -10, and FLOOR(-10.5) returns -11.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT TO_CHAR(hire_date, 'fmMonth DD, YYYY') AS hired
FROM employees
WHERE employee_id = 100;
If HIRE_DATE for this employee is June 17, 2003, what does this query display?

options.text: An error, because TO_CHAR cannot combine a month name with a day and year in one format model.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT salary + TO_NUMBER('1,000', '9,999') AS new_salary
FROM employees
WHERE employee_id = 100;
Which statement is true?

options.text: The statement executes successfully because the format model '9,999' matches the comma in the string.
The statement raises an error because TO_NUMBER does not accept a format model as a second argument.
The statement raises an error because commas are never allowed inside string literals passed to TO_NUMBER.
The statement silently ignores the comma and returns NULL.

solution: A - The statement executes successfully because the format model '9,999' matches the comma in the string.

options.text: It raises an error, because February never has 30 days in any year.
It returns March 1, 2024, because Oracle automatically rolls the date forward.
It returns February 28, 2024, ignoring the invalid day.
It returns NULL, because the day value is out of range.

solution: A - It raises an error, because February never has 30 days in any year.

options.text: February 29, 2024
March 2, 2024
February 31, 2024
An error, because January 31 has no equivalent day in February.

solution: A - February 29, 2024

question: Which two statements are true about the LAST_DAY and NEXT_DAY functions? (Choose TWO)

options.text: LAST_DAY(SYSDATE) returns the date of the final day of the current month.
NEXT_DAY(SYSDATE, 'MONDAY') can return the same date as SYSDATE if today is already Monday.
NEXT_DAY(SYSDATE, 'MONDAY') returns the date of the next Monday strictly after SYSDATE.
LAST_DAY requires a second argument specifying the month.
NEXT_DAY always returns a date in the same month as its input.

solution: A - LAST_DAY(SYSDATE) returns the date of the final day of the current month. C - NEXT_DAY(SYSDATE, 'MONDAY') returns the date of the next Monday strictly after SYSDATE.

options.text: A DATE value that is 7 days after HIRE_DATE.
A NUMBER representing 7 days in hours.
An error, because arithmetic cannot be performed directly on DATE columns.
A DATE value that is 7 months after HIRE_DATE.

solution: A - A DATE value that is 7 days after HIRE_DATE.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT department_id, job_id, SUM(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY ROLLUP(department_id, job_id);
Which statement is true about the result of this query?

options.text: It produces subtotal rows for each DEPARTMENT_ID and a grand total row, in addition to the detail rows for each DEPARTMENT_ID/JOB_ID combination.
It produces only the detail rows for each DEPARTMENT_ID/JOB_ID combination, identical to a plain GROUP BY.
It raises an error, because ROLLUP cannot be used with two columns.
It produces one row per JOB_ID only, ignoring DEPARTMENT_ID.

solution: A - It produces subtotal rows for each DEPARTMENT_ID and a grand total row, in addition to the detail rows for each DEPARTMENT_ID/JOB_ID combination.

question: Which statement correctly lists only the departments that have an average salary greater than 8000?

options.text: SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE AVG(salary) > 8000 GROUP BY department_id;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000 GROUP BY department_id;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id WHERE AVG(salary) > 8000;

solution: A - SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000;

question: Which statement is true about the HAVING clause in Oracle SQL?

options.text: HAVING can be used in a SELECT statement that contains only aggregate functions and no GROUP BY clause, treating the whole table as a single group.
HAVING must always be preceded by a GROUP BY clause in the same statement.
HAVING cannot reference a column that is not listed in the SELECT clause.
HAVING is evaluated before the WHERE clause.

solution: A - HAVING can be used in a SELECT statement that contains only aggregate functions and no GROUP BY clause, treating the whole table as a single group.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
CREATE VIEW emp_dept_90 AS
SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 90
WITH CHECK OPTION;
What happens if a user tries to UPDATE a row through EMP_DEPT_90, changing a value so that the row's DEPARTMENT_ID would effectively become 50?

options.text: Oracle rejects the update, because WITH CHECK OPTION prevents changes that would make the row disappear from the view's result set.
Oracle allows the update, and the row disappears from the view afterward.
Oracle allows the update, but automatically keeps DEPARTMENT_ID as 90 regardless of the new value.
WITH CHECK OPTION has no effect on UPDATE statements, only on INSERT statements.

solution: A - Oracle rejects the update, because WITH CHECK OPTION prevents changes that would make the row disappear from the view's result set.

question: Which two statements are true about views that are created WITH READ ONLY? (Choose TWO)

options.text: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements against the view are rejected by Oracle.
SELECT statements against the view still work normally.
WITH READ ONLY prevents the view from being queried by any user other than its owner.
WITH READ ONLY automatically makes the underlying base table read only as well.
A view created WITH READ ONLY cannot later be dropped.

solution: A - INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements against the view are rejected by Oracle. B - SELECT statements against the view still work normally.

question: Which view definition is NOT updatable through simple INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statements?

options.text: CREATE VIEW v1 AS SELECT department_id, SUM(salary) AS total FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
CREATE VIEW v2 AS SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = 60;
CREATE VIEW v3 AS SELECT * FROM employees;
CREATE VIEW v4 AS SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees WHERE salary > 5000;

solution: A - CREATE VIEW v1 AS SELECT department_id, SUM(salary) AS total FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;

question: Which statement about views in Oracle SQL is true?

options.text: A view does not store data itself; it stores a query definition that is executed whenever the view is referenced.
Creating a view always duplicates the data from the underlying table into a new physical segment.
A view can only be based on a single table, never on a join of multiple tables.
Dropping a view also drops the underlying base table.

solution: A - A view does not store data itself; it stores a query definition that is executed whenever the view is referenced.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
CREATE SEQUENCE order_seq
START WITH 100
INCREMENT BY 10
MAXVALUE 500
NOCYCLE;
What happens when ORDER_SEQ.NEXTVAL is selected for the first time, and then a second time, in the same session?

options.text: The first call returns 100, and the second call returns 110.
Both calls return 100, because NEXTVAL always returns the starting value until CURRVAL is used.
The first call returns 110, because the sequence skips the starting value.
The first call returns 100, and the second call raises an error unless CURRVAL is called in between.

solution: A - The first call returns 100, and the second call returns 110.

question: A new session connects to the database and has not yet referenced ORDER_SEQ.NEXTVAL. What happens if this session immediately queries ORDER_SEQ.CURRVAL?

options.text: Oracle raises an error, because CURRVAL is not defined for a session until NEXTVAL has been called at least once in that session.
Oracle returns the sequence's START WITH value.
Oracle returns NULL.
Oracle returns 0.

solution: A - Oracle raises an error, because CURRVAL is not defined for a session until NEXTVAL has been called at least once in that session.

question: Which two statements are true about sequences in Oracle SQL? (Choose TWO)

options.text: A sequence must be defined with the same column list as the single table it will supply values for.
CYCLE allows the sequence to restart from its MINVALUE (or MAXVALUE, for descending sequences) after reaching a limit.
A sequence automatically fills in gaps left by a ROLLBACK, guaranteeing no number is ever skipped.
DROP TABLE on the table that uses a sequence automatically drops the sequence as well.
CACHE 20 means Oracle pre-allocates and keeps 20 sequence values in memory for faster access.

solution: B - CYCLE allows the sequence to restart from its MINVALUE (or MAXVALUE, for descending sequences) after reaching a limit. E - CACHE 20 means Oracle pre-allocates and keeps 20 sequence values in memory for faster access.

question: Which statement correctly creates a public alias named EMP for the table HR.EMPLOYEES, so that any user in the database can refer to it simply as EMP?

options.text: CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM emp FOR hr.employees;
CREATE SYNONYM PUBLIC emp FOR hr.employees;
CREATE ALIAS emp FOR hr.employees;
CREATE PUBLIC VIEW emp FOR hr.employees;

solution: A - CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM emp FOR hr.employees;

question: Which statement is true about synonyms in Oracle SQL?

options.text: A synonym is simply an alternative name for a table, view, sequence, or other schema object; it does not store any data of its own.
Creating a synonym for a table automatically copies that table's data into the synonym.
A private synonym can be used by every user in the database, just like a public synonym.
A synonym can only be created for a table, never for a view or a sequence.

solution: A - A synonym is simply an alternative name for a table, view, sequence, or other schema object; it does not store any data of its own.

question: Which statement correctly removes the public synonym EMP?

options.text: DROP PUBLIC SYNONYM emp;
DROP SYNONYM PUBLIC emp;
DELETE PUBLIC SYNONYM emp;
DROP TABLE emp;

solution: A - DROP PUBLIC SYNONYM emp;

options.text: SCOTT gains the SELECT and INSERT privileges on HR.EMPLOYEES through the HR_CLERK role.
SCOTT becomes the owner of a new role called HR_CLERK.
The statements fail, because privileges cannot be granted to a role before the role has any members.
SCOTT can now grant the HR_CLERK role to other users, because granting a role always includes the ADMIN OPTION.

solution: A - SCOTT gains the SELECT and INSERT privileges on HR.EMPLOYEES through the HR_CLERK role.

question: Which statement is true about the difference between a role and a system privilege in Oracle?

options.text: A role is a named collection of privileges that can be granted to users as a single unit, which simplifies managing many privileges at once.
A role can only ever contain exactly one privilege.
System privileges must always be granted individually and can never be grouped together.
A role and a system privilege are simply two different names for the exact same concept in Oracle.

solution: A - A role is a named collection of privileges that can be granted to users as a single unit, which simplifies managing many privileges at once.

question: Which statement is true about indexes in Oracle SQL?

options.text: When a column is defined with a PRIMARY KEY constraint, Oracle automatically creates a unique index on that column.
Indexes make every DML statement (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) execute faster, with no additional overhead.
A table can have at most one index at any given time.
Creating an index copies and duplicates all the data from the indexed column into a new table.

solution: A - When a column is defined with a PRIMARY KEY constraint, Oracle automatically creates a unique index on that column.

question: Which two statements are true about indexes? (Choose TWO)

options.text: An index can speed up SELECT statements that filter or sort on the indexed column.
Dropping the table that an index is based on also drops the index automatically.
An index guarantees that the indexed column cannot contain duplicate values.
Indexes are required before a table can contain any rows.
Creating an index on a column prevents that column from ever being updated.

solution: A - An index can speed up SELECT statements that filter or sort on the indexed column. B - Dropping the table that an index is based on also drops the index automatically.

question: Which data dictionary view would a regular (non-DBA) user query to see the names and data types of the columns in a table that the user owns?

options.text: USER_TAB_COLUMNS
USER_CONSTRAINTS
ALL_USERS
USER_SEQUENCES

solution: A - USER_TAB_COLUMNS

question: Which statement is true about the ALL_, USER_, and DBA_ prefixes used in Oracle data dictionary views?

options.text: USER_ views show only objects owned by the current user; ALL_ views show objects the current user can access regardless of owner; DBA_ views show every object in the database and require elevated privileges.
DBA_ views show only objects owned by the current session, while USER_ views show every object in the database.
ALL_ views and USER_ views always return exactly the same rows for every user.
The three prefixes differ only in column names, never in which rows are returned.

solution: A - USER_ views show only objects owned by the current user; ALL_ views show objects the current user can access regardless of owner; DBA_ views show every object in the database and require elevated privileges.

question: Which data dictionary view would show the names of the constraints defined on a table owned by the current user, including their constraint type (for example, 'P' for primary key)?

options.text: USER_CONSTRAINTS
USER_TABLES
USER_INDEXES
USER_TRIGGERS

solution: A - USER_CONSTRAINTS

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT department_id FROM employees
MINUS
SELECT department_id FROM departments
WHERE location_id = 1700;
Which rows does this statement return?

options.text: The DEPARTMENT_ID values that appear in EMPLOYEES but do not appear among the departments located at LOCATION_ID 1700.
The DEPARTMENT_ID values that appear in both EMPLOYEES and the filtered DEPARTMENTS result.
The DEPARTMENT_ID values that appear in the filtered DEPARTMENTS result but not in EMPLOYEES.
An error, because MINUS cannot be combined with a WHERE clause in the second query.

solution: A - The DEPARTMENT_ID values that appear in EMPLOYEES but do not appear among the departments located at LOCATION_ID 1700.

options.text: The salary increase from the UPDATE is still in place, but the DELETE has been undone.
Both the UPDATE and the DELETE have been completely undone.
Both the UPDATE and the DELETE remain in effect, because ROLLBACK TO a savepoint has no effect on DML already executed.
The DELETE remains in effect, but the UPDATE has been undone.

solution: A - The salary increase from the UPDATE is still in place, but the DELETE has been undone.

question: Which two statements are true about transactions in Oracle SQL? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Executing a DDL statement such as CREATE TABLE implicitly commits any pending transaction.
A COMMIT statement makes all changes made during the current transaction permanent and visible to other sessions.
ROLLBACK can undo changes that another session has already committed.
A transaction can only ever contain exactly one DML statement.
SAVEPOINT permanently commits the changes made up to that point in the transaction.

solution: A - Executing a DDL statement such as CREATE TABLE implicitly commits any pending transaction. B - A COMMIT statement makes all changes made during the current transaction permanent and visible to other sessions.

question: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a system privilege and an object privilege in Oracle?

options.text: A system privilege (such as CREATE TABLE) allows a user to perform an action in the database generally, while an object privilege (such as SELECT on a specific table) controls access to one particular object.
An object privilege allows a user to create new users, while a system privilege only allows querying data.
System privileges can only be granted by the object's owner, never by a DBA.
Object privileges and system privileges are granted using different SQL statements that cannot both be called GRANT.

solution: A - A system privilege (such as CREATE TABLE) allows a user to perform an action in the database generally, while an object privilege (such as SELECT on a specific table) controls access to one particular object.

options.text: HR can grant the SELECT privilege on ORDERS to other users.
HR automatically becomes the new owner of the ORDERS table.
HR can modify the structure of the ORDERS table using ALTER TABLE.
WITH GRANT OPTION has no practical effect on object privileges, only on system privileges.

solution: A - HR can grant the SELECT privilege on ORDERS to other users.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
MERGE INTO employees_bonus b
USING employees e
ON (b.employee_id = e.employee_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET b.bonus = e.salary * 0.1
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (employee_id, bonus) VALUES (e.employee_id, e.salary * 0.1);
What is the purpose of this statement?

options.text: It updates the bonus for employees who already exist in EMPLOYEES_BONUS, and inserts a new bonus row for employees who do not yet exist there.
It deletes rows from EMPLOYEES_BONUS that do not match any row in EMPLOYEES.
It only inserts new rows, ignoring the WHEN MATCHED clause entirely.
It raises an error, because MERGE cannot combine an UPDATE and an INSERT in the same statement.

solution: A - It updates the bonus for employees who already exist in EMPLOYEES_BONUS, and inserts a new bonus row for employees who do not yet exist there.

question: Which statement correctly copies every row from DEPARTMENTS into DEPARTMENTS_BACKUP, assuming both tables already exist with compatible columns, without using a loop?

options.text: INSERT INTO departments_backup SELECT * FROM departments;
INSERT INTO departments_backup VALUES (SELECT * FROM departments);
INSERT departments_backup FROM departments;
COPY INTO departments_backup FROM departments;

solution: A - INSERT INTO departments_backup SELECT * FROM departments;

question: Which two statements are true about the ALTER TABLE command in Oracle SQL? (Choose TWO)

options.text: ALTER TABLE ... ADD can be used to add one or more new columns to an existing table.
ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY can be used to change the data type or size of an existing column, subject to the existing data being compatible with the change.
ALTER TABLE can never be used to remove a column once the table contains data.
ALTER TABLE automatically commits any uncommitted DML from other sessions.
ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN can remove the last remaining column of a table.

solution: A - ALTER TABLE ... ADD can be used to add one or more new columns to an existing table. B - ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY can be used to change the data type or size of an existing column, subject to the existing data being compatible with the change.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
CREATE TABLE emp_summary AS
SELECT employee_id, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 80;
Which statement is true about the EMP_SUMMARY table after this statement executes?

options.text: EMP_SUMMARY is a new table containing a copy of the selected rows and columns, but it does not inherit the PRIMARY KEY or FOREIGN KEY constraints of EMPLOYEES.
EMP_SUMMARY is a view, not a real table, and always reflects the current data in EMPLOYEES.
EMP_SUMMARY automatically has the same constraints and indexes as the EMPLOYEES table.
The statement fails, because CREATE TABLE cannot be combined with a SELECT statement.

solution: A - EMP_SUMMARY is a new table containing a copy of the selected rows and columns, but it does not inherit the PRIMARY KEY or FOREIGN KEY constraints of EMPLOYEES.

question: Which statement is true about CHECK constraints in Oracle SQL?

options.text: A CHECK constraint can reference only the columns of the row being inserted or updated; it cannot reference SYSDATE, USER, or another row's values.
A CHECK constraint can be used to guarantee that a column's value matches a value in another table.
A CHECK constraint can reference the pseudocolumn ROWNUM to limit how many rows satisfy the condition.
A table can have at most one CHECK constraint in total.

solution: A - A CHECK constraint can reference only the columns of the row being inserted or updated; it cannot reference SYSDATE, USER, or another row's values.

question: Which statement correctly defines a composite primary key on the columns ORDER_ID and PRODUCT_ID in a new table?

options.text: CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id NUMBER, product_id NUMBER, quantity NUMBER, CONSTRAINT order_items_pk PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id));
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, product_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, quantity NUMBER);
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id NUMBER, product_id NUMBER, quantity NUMBER, PRIMARY KEY order_id, product_id);
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id NUMBER, product_id NUMBER, quantity NUMBER, CONSTRAINT order_items_pk COMPOSITE KEY (order_id, product_id));

solution: A - CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id NUMBER, product_id NUMBER, quantity NUMBER, CONSTRAINT order_items_pk PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id));

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT last_name, salary, department_id
FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary)
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id = e.department_id
);
Which statement is true about this query?

options.text: It is a correlated subquery, because the inner query references DEPARTMENT_ID from the outer query and is re-evaluated for each row processed by the outer query.
It is a non-correlated subquery that is evaluated exactly once before the outer query runs.
It raises an error, because a subquery in the WHERE clause cannot reference a column from the outer query.
It returns every employee, because AVG(salary) is always greater than any individual SALARY value.

solution: A - It is a correlated subquery, because the inner query references DEPARTMENT_ID from the outer query and is re-evaluated for each row processed by the outer query.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT e.last_name AS employee, m.last_name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
What does this statement illustrate?

options.text: A self join, where the EMPLOYEES table is joined to itself to match each employee with the last name of their manager.
A cross join that produces the Cartesian product of EMPLOYEES with itself.
An outer join that returns employees even when MANAGER_ID is NULL, showing NULL for the manager's name.
A syntax error, because a table cannot be joined to itself in Oracle SQL.

solution: A - A self join, where the EMPLOYEES table is joined to itself to match each employee with the last name of their manager.

question: Which two statements are true about implicit data type conversion in Oracle SQL? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Oracle can implicitly convert a VARCHAR2 value such as '100' to a NUMBER when it is used in an arithmetic expression.
Oracle can implicitly convert a VARCHAR2 value such as 'ABC' to a NUMBER without raising an error.
Oracle can implicitly convert a DATE value to a VARCHAR2 using the session's default date format when necessary.
Implicit conversion never occurs in Oracle; every conversion must use an explicit function such as TO_NUMBER.
Oracle always prefers implicit conversion over raising an error, even when the string clearly cannot represent a number.

solution: A - Oracle can implicitly convert a VARCHAR2 value such as '100' to a NUMBER when it is used in an arithmetic expression. C - Oracle can implicitly convert a DATE value to a VARCHAR2 using the session's default date format when necessary.
